name: OpenMausBot
tagline: A chat app where every contact is an AI bot with its own computer and apps - the open-source alternative to Grok Bot.
sentence: Gives you a team of AI bots in a familiar chat interface, each with its own computer and app connections, that ask permission before doing anything risky.

visual.alt: The OpenMausBot desktop app showing a chat interface with an AI bot conversation on the right and a contact list of bots on the left, similar to a messaging app like iMessage or WhatsApp.
visual.caption: Each 'contact' is an AI bot with its own computer - send it a task the way you'd send a text.

board.say: You want AI agents to handle tasks (inbox sweeps, competitor watches, code reviews) but don't want to give them free rein on your machine.
Send a message to a bot in the chat interface, or set a schedule, a webhook (an automatic trigger from another app), or an app-event trigger.
A task in plain language, like 'Sweep my inbox and draft replies to anything from clients.'
The bot works in its own isolated computer and asks permission before risky actions.
steps: The bot works in its own isolated computer (a cloud desktop, a local virtual machine, or your host)
When it needs to do something risky (run a shell command, edit a file), it shows an Allow/Deny card
It can connect to Gmail, Slack, GitHub, Notion, and hundreds of other apps

board.say: The task done, with a full transcript and approval cards for everything risky.

outputs.eg: A weekly competitor watch that runs on schedule and posts a summary to Slack
Before sending an email or running a command, the bot shows Allow/Deny - you decide

before: You run AI tasks in separate terminal windows with no approval step before risky actions
Each agent has its own interface - switching between Claude, Codex, and Grok means switching apps
after: One chat app, multiple agents, each with approval cards before risky actions
Schedule recurring tasks (weekly reports, inbox sweeps) and get results in chat
uses_note: The project is 87 days old and describes itself as 'Early but real.' No published case studies or independent user reports found.

coverage.title: Best Open Source Grok Bot Alternatives

steps: Download the [desktop app](https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot/releases) for Mac, Windows, or Ubuntu
During onboarding, it detects your installed agent CLIs (Claude Code, Codex, Grok)
Send a message to a bot and try a simple task like 'Summarize the last 5 emails in my inbox'
try.paste:
/skillspector https://github.com/milind-soni/OpenMausBot
Then: Download the desktop app from GitHub Releases, let onboarding detect your agents, and try a simple task. 10 minutes.

footprint.disk: no data found (Electron app with bundled dependencies)
footprint.memory: no data found (runs a local server on port 8799)
footprint.runs_on: macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel, signed .dmg), Windows (x64, unsigned installer), Ubuntu 24.04 (beta, .deb or AppImage). Node 24+ for building from source.

best_for: Anyone who wants one chat app to manage multiple AI agents with built-in permission controls
People who already pay for AI coding agents and want a visual interface instead of terminals
Non-technical users who want to schedule recurring AI tasks without writing code
skip_if: You're comfortable in the terminal - OpenMausBot adds a GUI layer you may not need
You want a polished product today - it's self-described as early with rough edges
You're on Ubuntu with Wayland - host control is disabled on that setup

alternatives.name: T3 Code
alternatives.line: A similar multi-agent dashboard focused on coding - more mature, with mobile apps

alternatives.name: Grok Bot
alternatives.line: The closed-source original - polished but locked to xAI's ecosystem

watch: **Early stage.** Self-described as 'Early but real' with rough edges expected.
**Windows installer is unsigned.** SmartScreen will show a warning on install - you'll need to click 'Run anyway.'
**Ubuntu is beta.** Host control is disabled on Wayland (the default display system on newer Ubuntu).
**API keys stored in plain text** in `config.json` (with restricted file permissions on Mac and Linux, but readable on Windows).
